title: Redwood POC weekly sync - Quantaco AI - cost econ
summary: Weekly POC sync to review pilot performance and unit economics. Discussed tokens/sec/$ benchmarks, observed caching savings from prefix reuse, batching tradeoffs for tail latency, and a proposed tuning plan. Action items: run 24h sustained benchmark at 95th perc latency target, share updated cost model spreadsheet, and schedule an infra test for on-prem variant. Customer remains cautious about tail latency and regulatory logging requirements.
topics: 1) Benchmarks overview (tokens/sec/$) 2) Caching observed savings 3) Batching and latency tradeoffs 4) Deployment options (dedicated vs hosted) 5) Next steps and action items
next_steps: Redwood to run 24h stress run with live traffic profile and share raw logs (Rafael) - due 2026-11-10
Quantaco to confirm list of 10 representative customer prompts for quality checks - Priya - due 2026-11-09
Redwood to send updated cost model spreadsheet with caching scenarios - Maya - due 2026-11-06
Schedule infra test for on-prem private node with KMS integration - Anika/Maya - tentative week of 2026-11-16
action_items: Rafael Ortiz: run 24h sustained benchmark against prod-like prompt mix; include tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, and cost per 1M tokens - due 2026-11-10
Maya Chen: share revised cost/unit economics spreadsheet with tokenization assumptions and caching columns - due 2026-11-06
Priya Desai: provide canonical prompt set and success criteria for quality regressions - due 2026-11-09
Tom Becker: provide access/notes for on-prem eval (network, KMS) - due 2026-11-12
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is the weekly POC sync for Quantaco, we just want to go over the numbers from last week's test and the cost econ side. Uh, Rafael is going to run through the benchmark.
[00:18] Rafael Ortiz: Cool thanks Maya. Quick context - we ran a mixed workload for 6 hours on the dedicated pool: a 50/30/20 split of short prompts, medium, and long. Observed sustained tokens per second around 28k on average with peak bursts hitting ~42k for a few minutes. Cost per million tokens ended up at about $2.40 in the baseline config.
[00:41] Priya Desai: Sorry can I ask, that $2.40, is that with caching turned on?
[00:45] Rafael Ortiz: Good call. So that's baseline with prefix caching enabled on short prompts - the caching saved about 35% of token generation on those repeated query prefixes. If we disable caching the cost goes up to about $3.70 per million.
[01:02] Liam O'Connor: Wait, 35% seems high - is that from KV cache hits or from request-level dedupe?
[01:07] Rafael Ortiz: It's mostly KV/prefix cache hits. Our workload had a lot of repeated starts - e.g., the 'summarize the following' starter - so we saw a bunch of shared keys in the first 32 tokens which avoided re-computation.
[01:20] Sara Wu: There's also the question of how that'll change under more diverse production traffic. We don't have that many repeated prefixes in the wild.
[01:26] Rafael Ortiz: Totally - that's why we pushed the mixed workload. We also ran a 95th-percentile latency calc. With batching enabled at default batch window of 10ms we saw p95 around 210ms for short prompts, p95 jumped to 560ms for medium due to combining batching with longer decode times.
[01:44] Tom Becker: So is it correct to say batching improved throughput but increased p95?
[01:48] Rafael Ortiz: Exactly. Tokens/sec went up ~1.8x with batching on, which reduced overall cost per 1M tokens by ~28%, but the tradeoff is tail latency - for customer-facing interactive flows you might want smaller batch windows or token-aware batching to keep p95 lower.
[02:02] Priya Desai: What about the dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs? Earlier you suggested dedicated might be better for predictability.
[02:08] Maya Chen: Right - Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity which makes sustained throughput predictable. Hosted is cheaper for bursty loads because you pay the per-token, but latency and cold-start variability can be higher. For your SLA needs where p95 matters, Dedicated with tuned batching or hybrid routing (low-latency tier to hosted fallback) is common.
[02:28] Liam O'Connor: How much does quantization affect those numbers? If we quantize to 4-bit for the v-model we use, does tokens/sec change a lot?
[02:35] Rafael Ortiz: We ran a q4 benchmark - tokens/sec improved ~22% on the same hardware and cost per token dropped another ~12% because memory bandwidth improved. But note small quality deltas on certain hallucination-prone prompts; so you need to run your quality checks.
[02:52] Priya Desai: Can you quantify caching savings in the spreadsheet format? I want to show product leadership the ranges.
[02:57] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll update the cost model with three scenarios: no caching, prefix-KV caching at observed 35% for our current test, and optimistic caching at 50% for very repeated workloads.
[03:10] Sara Wu: For the batching tradeoff, would token-aware batching help? Like groups by prefix and estimate remaining sequence length?
[03:16] Rafael Ortiz: We have token-aware batching heuristics in Redwood Optimize, it helps a lot. In our internal tests it cut the p95 penalty in half while retaining most throughput gains. We'll include that in the config we run next.
[03:31] Liam O'Connor: One concern is the tail when you combine long and short prompts in the same batch - the short prompts wait for the long ones.
[03:36] Rafael Ortiz: Yeah that's the classic head-of-line blocking. Our batching has options: separate lanes for short and long, or speculative micro-batching (flush small batches if waiting too long). For real-time flows we usually isolate short prompt lanes.
[03:48] Priya Desai: On the security front, a couple questions - our compliance team wants to see audit logs and KMS integration for the private eval.
[03:55] Anika Patel: We can share the security pack; Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and detailed audit logs. We'll need network details for the on-prem node; Tom can share that after the call.
[04:07] Tom Becker: I'll send a runbook and network constraints. Also want to try the on-prem node with our internal CI to see if the latency characteristics match.
[04:14] Rafael Ortiz: Great - note that on-prem gives you the least network variable but you're also responsible for kernel and driver updates; we provide the deployment package.
[04:24] Maya Chen: Back to cost econ - Liam, do you have any target for tokens/sec or cost per 1M tokens that your finance team uses?
[04:31] Liam O'Connor: Finance wants to see sub-$2 per 1M tokens for our base case. We can stretch to $2.20 if p95 is <250ms for short user interactions.
[04:40] Rafael Ortiz: In our tuning scenario with token-aware batching, q4 quantization, and current cache hit rate (35%), we project $1.85 per 1M tokens and p95 at ~230ms for short prompts. That's within the stretch number.
[04:52] Priya Desai: How confident are you in the projection? Any assumptions that could shift cost materially?
[04:57] Rafael Ortiz: The projection hinges on three main variables: cache hit rate (if that drops to 10% cost goes up ~25%), sustained utilization (we assumed 70% sustained), and quantization acceptance (if you can't quantize then remove that benefit). We'll put sensitivity columns in the spreadsheet.
[05:14] Sara Wu: Regarding the sensitivity, can you show a scenario where we prioritize latency over cost - say targeting p95 < 200ms?
[05:20] Maya Chen: Yes we have a high-performance profile: smaller batch windows, dedicated short-prompt lanes, and higher over-provisioning - that raises cost to about $2.40 per 1M tokens but gets p95 below 200ms most of the time.
[05:33] Tom Becker: For the on-prem test, will we be able to toggle quantization easily? We want to A/B test quality.
[05:39] Rafael Ortiz: Yes toggles are simple; we can deploy multiple model variants and route a percentage of traffic. We'll also keep model version pinning so you can rollback.
[05:48] Priya Desai: Ok, next I want to call out a small issue - during the first hour last week we saw 4 errors per minute from the adapter layer, looks like timeouts around tokenization step. Any idea?
[05:59] Rafael Ortiz: We traced that to a spike in concurrent small requests that hit a transient issue in our tokenization service - we applied a retry and increased the tokenizer pool and error rate dropped to near zero. We'll include the traces.
[06:12] Liam O'Connor: Could that tokenizer be a single point of failure for us on Dedicated?
[06:16] Rafael Ortiz: It's possible if you run a custom tokenization pipeline; Redwood uses a horizontally scalable tokenizer pool but for extreme scale we recommend co-locating tokenizers or using our dedicated tokenizer instances.
[06:29] Maya Chen: Alright, quick recap before we wrap: Rafael will run the 24h sustained benchmark with token-aware batching and q4 quant; Maya will send an updated cost model with scenarios; Priya will share canonical prompts; Tom will provide on-prem network notes. We'll meet same time next week to review results.
[06:46] Priya Desai: Sounds good. Anything else on open items?
[06:49] Sara Wu: One more - can we get a sample of the raw logs in S3-like format so our infra can ingest?
[06:55] Anika Patel: Yes, we'll generate a sanitized sample and share a link.
[07:00] Maya Chen: Perfect, thanks everyone.
[07:03] Priya Desai: Thanks all.
[07:05] (call ends)
notes: Transcript has occasional mis-hears (e.g., 'Redwood Dedication' vs 'Dedicated') and some speaker label jitter; timestamps approximate. Customer emphasis on p95 tail latency and finance target of sub-$2 per 1M tokens. Next run will test token-aware batching + quantization and produce sensitivity analysis.
